questions.subtopic: 1D1 Fraud triangle, fraud risks and schemes. Fraud or error
questions.question: Internal auditor Yasmine finds twelve duplicate supplier payments at a Moroccan freight company. Which additional fact would MOST strongly point to fraud instead of error?

options.A: The duplicates exceed the amount set for reporting errors
options.B: The clerk altered invoice numbers so the duplicate check passed
options.C: The same clerk entered every one of the duplicate payments
options.D: The system's duplicate check was offline during a software upgrade

questions.key_concept: Intent separates fraud from error: fraud is a deliberate act, usually shown by deceit or an effort to conceal.
questions.pre_read: Ask which fact shows a deliberate choice to hide something, and which facts an honest mistake could also explain.
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards' glossary treats fraud as a deliberate act involving deceit or concealment, carried out to gain an advantage. Changing invoice numbers to slip past a check is a chosen step to keep the payments from being noticed, so it points to intent. One clerk entering every duplicate is the runner-up, but repeated honest mistakes look the same; that pattern is a reason to look closer, not a sign of deception.

wrong_explanations.A: Size is not the test. The glossary's description of fraud sets no minimum amount, and a large duplicate can still be an honest mistake.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: one person behind every duplicate deserves a closer look, but repeated honest mistakes look the same. Nothing here shows deceit or concealment.
wrong_explanations.D: A check that was offline explains how duplicates got through by accident. It shows a control gap, not an intention to deceive.

tips: Eliminate: A, because fraud has no minimum amount, and D, because a failed check explains how an honest mistake got through.
Final two: B beats C because altering records to avoid a check shows deliberate concealment; one clerk's repeated entries could still be honest mistakes.
Exam cue: when asked what separates fraud from error, look for the option showing intent, usually an effort to conceal the act.

questions.subtopic: 1D1 Fraud triangle, fraud risks and schemes. The triangle side a control reaches
questions.question: An internal auditor notes that a Bogota clinic's cashier both records and pays refunds, and that cashier pay was recently cut. Management's plan to split the two tasks would MOST directly reduce which fraud condition?

options.A: The motivation created by the recent cut in pay
options.B: The rationalization that small refunds harm nobody
options.C: The chance that two cashiers collude on refunds
options.D: The opportunity to take cash unseen

questions.key_concept: Of the fraud triangle's three conditions, process controls such as divided duties act mainly on opportunity.
questions.pre_read: Name the three conditions of the fraud triangle first, then ask which one a change in who does what can alter.
questions.correct_explanation: The fraud triangle, as the CIA syllabus lists it, has three conditions: motivation, opportunity and rationalization. Dividing a task between two people is a control, and controls work on opportunity: no single cashier can now both create a refund and pay it out. The pay cut is the runner-up because it is real pressure, but splitting tasks changes what a person can do, not why they might want to.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the pay cut is real motivation, but dividing tasks does nothing about pay. Pressure sits with people; controls narrow what they can do unseen.
wrong_explanations.B: Rationalization is the excuse a person uses to feel justified. Changing who performs a task does not change that excuse; culture and leaders' example do.
wrong_explanations.C: Dividing tasks does not reduce collusion. Collusion is the weak point of the control, because two people acting together can still get past it.

tips: Eliminate: B, because an excuse lives in attitudes that task design does not touch, and C, because collusion is what defeats divided duties.
Final two: D beats A because separating duties removes the chance to act alone and unseen; the pay cut and its pressure stay unchanged.
Exam cue: on fraud triangle questions, match process controls such as divided duties and approvals to opportunity.

questions.subtopic: 1D1 Fraud triangle, fraud risks and schemes. Fraud for the organization's benefit
questions.question: A sales director at a Thai machinery maker bribes a customer's buyer to win an order and books the payment as marketing, gaining nothing personally. How should internal auditor Niran BEST classify the act?

options.A: As fraud committed to gain an unlawful business advantage
options.B: As a commercial decision outside the meaning of fraud
options.C: As a recording error in the marketing expense account
options.D: As a conflict of interest held by the sales director

questions.key_concept: Fraud can be committed for the organization as well as against it: the advantage sought may be personal or for the business.
questions.pre_read: Notice who benefits from the act, then ask whether the meaning of fraud depends on who benefits.
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards' glossary treats fraud as a deliberate, deceptive act by a person or an organization to win an unfair or unlawful advantage, and that advantage can be personal or for the business. A hidden bribe booked as marketing fits. Calling it a commercial decision is the runner-up, but benefit to the company does not take an act out of the meaning of fraud.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the company gains, yet the glossary's meaning of fraud covers an unlawful advantage for the business as well as for a person.
wrong_explanations.C: An error is unintended. The director chose to pay the buyer and to disguise the payment, so the wrong account is concealment, not a slip.
wrong_explanations.D: A conflict of interest needs a competing personal interest. The director gains nothing personally; the deception is what matters here.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the mislabeled entry was deliberate, and D, because the director has no competing personal interest in the order.
Final two: A beats B because the meaning of fraud covers an unlawful advantage for the organization, not only personal gain.
Exam cue: fraud can be committed for the organization as well as against it; who benefits does not decide the label.

questions.subtopic: 1D1 Fraud triangle, fraud risks and schemes. Fraud risk where no money moves
questions.question: Internal auditor Katrin is planning an engagement on safety inspection records at an Icelandic airline maintenance unit that pays bonuses for fast turnaround and handles no money. Which fraud risk should Katrin MOST clearly recognize?

options.A: No fraud risk worth recording in a unit without cash
options.B: Purchasing fraud in the airline's separate spare-parts department
options.C: Inspection sign-offs falsified to protect turnaround bonuses
options.D: Honest recording mistakes made under turnaround pressure

questions.key_concept: Fraud risk is not limited to cash and assets: information can be falsified on purpose to gain an unfair advantage.
questions.pre_read: Ask what could be deliberately falsified in this activity, and who would gain from it.
questions.correct_explanation: Fraud is any deliberate deception for an unfair advantage, and the glossary's description names forgery and misuse of information as well as assets. A bonus tied to speed gives staff a reason to sign off inspections that were not done. Standard 13.2 requires fraud risk to be considered in every engagement. Looking at purchasing is the runner-up, but it follows the money and misses the records under review.

wrong_explanations.A: Fraud does not need cash. The glossary's description covers deceit, forgery and misuse of information for an unfair advantage, such as a bonus.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: purchasing does carry fraud risk, but it is another department's activity. The records under review can themselves be falsified for gain.
wrong_explanations.D: A mistake made under turnaround pressure is an error, because nothing is intended. The question asks for a fraud risk, which needs a deliberate act.

tips: Eliminate: A, because fraud covers falsified information as well as stolen assets, and D, because an honest mistake has no intent.
Final two: C beats B because the fraud risk to weigh sits in the activity under review; falsified records can earn a bonus without any cash moving.
Exam cue: when a process handles no money, ask what information could be falsified and who would gain from it.

questions.subtopic: 1D2 Weighing fraud risk in an engagement. Fraud in every engagement risk assessment
questions.question: Internal auditor Eero is planning an assurance engagement on bus maintenance efficiency at a Finnish city, and the fleet manager says fraud belongs in fraud audits. How should Eero BEST treat fraud risk?

options.A: Leave it to the organization's separate investigations unit
options.B: Add it once the fleet manager agrees it is relevant
options.C: Consider specific fraud risks in the engagement risk assessment
options.D: Consider it later if fieldwork testing turns up unusual transactions

questions.key_concept: Every engagement risk assessment must consider fraud risk, during planning, whatever the engagement is called.
questions.pre_read: Notice the engagement's label and the manager's view, then ask whether either one changes what planning must cover.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.2 Engagement Risk Assessment makes considering specific fraud risks part of identifying the risks to review in every engagement, whatever its label. It happens during planning so that it can shape the objectives, scope and tests. Waiting for odd transactions is the runner-up, but by then the work program was built without asking how fraud could occur in maintenance.

wrong_explanations.A: An investigations unit handles suspected cases. It does not remove the internal auditor's duty to consider fraud risk when assessing this engagement's risks.
wrong_explanations.B: In an assurance engagement the internal auditors decide which risks to assess. Considering fraud risk does not wait for the manager's agreement.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: testing may reveal fraud signs, but the requirement is to consider fraud risk while planning, before objectives, scope and tests are set.

tips: Eliminate: A, because another unit's cases do not replace the engagement risk assessment, and B, because management does not decide which risks an assurance engagement weighs.
Final two: C beats D because Standard 13.2 puts fraud risk into planning for every engagement; it is not triggered by what testing later finds.
Exam cue: 'in a fraud audit', 'if management asks' and 'after fieldwork' are wrong timings; fraud risk is considered in every engagement's planning.

questions.subtopic: 1D2 Weighing fraud risk in an engagement. Advisory work and fraud risk
questions.question: Managers at an Omani logistics firm ask internal auditor Badr for informal advice on a new expense app, under terms that call for no written risk assessment. How should Badr BEST handle fraud risk?

options.A: Weigh how the app could enable fraud, without a formal assessment
options.B: Prepare a full documented fraud risk assessment before advising
options.C: Treat fraud risk as outside the scope of advisory work
options.D: Let the requesting managers decide whether fraud matters here

questions.key_concept: In advisory work the agreement may remove the formal, documented risk assessment, but due professional care still weighs fraud.
questions.pre_read: Separate two things: whether fraud is thought about, and how formally that thinking has to be recorded.
questions.correct_explanation: Due professional care under Standard 4.2 includes weighing the chance of fraud in any service, advisory work included. Standard 13.2 adds that for advisory services a formal, written risk assessment may be unnecessary, depending on what was agreed, and here the terms call for none. A full documented assessment is the runner-up: thorough, but it applies the assurance routine against the agreed terms.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: thorough, but Standard 13.2 lets the agreement decide whether advisory work needs a formal, documented assessment, and these terms call for none.
wrong_explanations.C: Advisory services are still internal audit services. Due professional care, including weighing the chance of fraud, applies to them as well.
wrong_explanations.D: The managers agree the nature and scope of the advice. Whether the internal auditor exercises due professional care is not theirs to waive.

tips: Eliminate: C, because due professional care covers advisory work too, and D, because the requesting managers cannot waive the auditor's care.
Final two: A beats B because Standard 13.2 lets the agreement remove the formal, documented assessment for advisory work, while fraud is still weighed.
Exam cue: in advisory work the formality of the risk assessment may drop by agreement; the thinking about fraud does not.

questions.subtopic: 1D2 Weighing fraud risk in an engagement. Ranking processes by fraud exposure
questions.question: At a Panamanian port authority, crane procurement has the largest budget and three independent approvers; one clerk alone approves and pays daily cash refunds. How should internal auditor Itzel BEST rank their fraud exposure?

options.A: By the annual amount passing through each process
options.B: By the number of frauds detected in each process to date
options.C: By each process manager's own rating of their fraud risk
options.D: By the likelihood and impact of fraud in each process

questions.key_concept: Fraud risks are prioritized by significance, which combines how likely the fraud is with how much harm it would do.
questions.pre_read: For each process, note what is at stake and how easily one person could act unseen, then ask what a ranking must combine.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.2 requires internal auditors to evaluate the significance of the risks they identify and to prioritize them, and the glossary says significance is typically judged by impact and likelihood. The refund process moves less money, but one clerk controls it from start to finish, so fraud is more likely there. Ranking by annual amount is the runner-up: it measures impact and leaves likelihood out.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the amount at stake matters, but it is the impact half. A smaller process that one person controls can be far more exposed.
wrong_explanations.B: Fraud is concealed, so few known cases says little about exposure. A clean record may mean that nothing has been caught yet.
wrong_explanations.C: Management's view is useful input, but managers rarely suspect their own area. The internal auditor forms an independent judgment of significance.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a clean record does not show low exposure when fraud is concealed, and C, because management's self-rating is input, not the auditor's judgment.
Final two: D beats A because significance combines likelihood with impact; a large budget with strong approvals can rank below a small process one clerk controls.
Exam cue: when processes are compared for fraud exposure, weigh both how likely and how costly, not size or history alone.

questions.subtopic: 1D2 Weighing fraud risk in an engagement. Updating an earlier risk assessment
questions.question: Internal auditor Isla is planning a repeat engagement on rent refunds at a Scottish housing association, where last year's engagement risk assessment found no fraud. What should Isla do about fraud risk FIRST?

options.A: Reuse last year's assessment exactly as it stands for this engagement
options.B: Review and update last year's assessment, fraud risks included
options.C: Build a new assessment and set last year's work aside
options.D: Omit fraud risk this year, given last year's clean result

questions.key_concept: For an activity assessed before, the earlier engagement risk assessment is reviewed and updated, and fraud risk stays in it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what may have changed in a year, and whether a clean result last time says anything about this time.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.2 says that when the relevant risks of an activity were identified in an earlier engagement, the internal auditors need only review and update that assessment. Updating keeps fraud risk in view, because staff, systems and pressures change in a year. Reusing the old assessment untouched is the runner-up: it saves time but skips the review that the requirement still asks for.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the earlier work can be used, but the requirement is to review and update it. Unchanged reuse assumes nothing moved in a year.
wrong_explanations.C: Starting again is more than Standard 13.2 asks. For an activity assessed before, a review and update of the earlier assessment is enough.
wrong_explanations.D: A clean result last year is not evidence of low fraud risk now. Fraud is concealed by design, and every engagement considers it.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the earlier assessment may be reviewed and updated instead of rebuilt, and D, because last year's clean result does not remove fraud risk.
Final two: B beats A because the requirement is review and update; conditions and fraud risks can change even when the process looks the same.
Exam cue: for a repeat engagement, the earlier risk assessment is a starting point to refresh, not a reason to skip fraud.

questions.subtopic: 1D3 Fraud risk management and red flags. A missing fraud response plan
questions.question: Evaluating fraud risk management at a Uruguayan dairy cooperative, internal auditor Camila finds a hotline and an anti-fraud policy, but nothing stating who investigates a report. What should Camila recommend as MOST important?

options.A: That management define roles in a fraud response plan
options.B: That internal audit lead the investigation of hotline reports
options.C: That the hotline close until an investigator is appointed
options.D: That internal audit write and own the response procedures

questions.key_concept: An organization should have a fraud response plan saying who does what when fraud is suspected; adopting it is management's job.
questions.pre_read: Find the gap in the program first, then ask who should close it and who should only assess it.
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's position paper on fraud says an organization should have a fraud response plan that sets out its policies and investigation methods and makes internal audit's role clear when fraud is suspected. The plan is management's to adopt. Naming internal audit as the investigator is the runner-up, but the paper says investigating is not normally internal audit's task and needs specific experience.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it fills the gap, but investigating is not normally internal audit's task. It depends on the mandate and on having the specific skills.
wrong_explanations.C: Closing the hotline removes a channel for detecting fraud. The gap is the missing plan for handling reports, not the channel itself.
wrong_explanations.D: Internal auditors advise on and assess the plan. Writing and owning management's procedures would be a management responsibility and weaken later assurance.

tips: Eliminate: C, because closing a detection channel adds risk, and D, because internal auditors assess management's procedures instead of owning them.
Final two: A beats B because management sets who responds to suspected fraud; internal audit investigates only where its mandate and skills allow.
Exam cue: a policy and a hotline are not a full program; look for a response plan that says who does what when fraud is suspected.

questions.subtopic: 1D3 Fraud risk management and red flags. Who is responsible for preventing fraud
questions.question: Internal auditor Aigerim reviews a draft anti-fraud policy at a Kazakh rail operator. Which sentence about internal audit should Aigerim challenge as LEAST consistent with the function's role?

options.A: Internal audit assesses the controls that prevent and detect fraud
options.B: Internal audit considers fraud risk in planning each engagement
options.C: Internal audit may investigate where its mandate and skills allow
options.D: Internal audit is responsible for preventing fraud in operations

questions.key_concept: Management is responsible for preventing fraud; internal audit assesses the anti-fraud controls and considers fraud risk in its work.
questions.pre_read: For each sentence, ask whether it has internal audit assessing and advising, or doing management's job.
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's position paper on fraud says that preventing fraud is management's responsibility, not a direct duty of internal audit. Internal audit's part is to assess the controls and weigh fraud risk in its plan and engagements. The sentence on investigating is the runner-up, since investigating is not a typical internal audit task, but it is acceptable once tied to mandate and skills.

wrong_explanations.A: This sentence fits. Assessing the controls meant to prevent and detect fraud is the role the position paper gives internal audit.
wrong_explanations.B: This sentence fits. Standard 13.2 requires internal auditors to consider specific fraud risks when assessing the risks of each engagement.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: investigating is not normally internal audit's task, but this sentence is conditional on mandate and skills, which the position paper accepts.

tips: Eliminate: A, because assessing anti-fraud controls is internal audit's stated role, and B, because Standard 13.2 requires fraud risk to be considered in each engagement.
Final two: D beats C because prevention belongs to management, while investigating is acceptable for internal audit when the mandate and competencies are there.
Exam cue: management prevents and responds; internal audit assesses, advises and reports. A sentence handing prevention to internal audit is the odd one out.

questions.subtopic: 1D3 Fraud risk management and red flags. Weighing an explanation for a red flag
questions.question: At a Sri Lankan tea exporter, the warehouse manager tells internal auditor Dilani that stock write-offs tripled because of monsoon damage. What should Dilani do FIRST?

options.A: Accept the explanation and note it in the workpapers
options.B: Seek evidence from independent sources that tests the explanation
options.C: Obtain the manager's signed statement confirming the explanation
options.D: Report that the manager is concealing the theft of stock

questions.key_concept: Professional skepticism means testing what management says against independent evidence before relying on it or drawing a conclusion.
questions.pre_read: Ask who supplied the explanation, and whether each option adds evidence from anyone else.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 4.3 Professional Skepticism requires internal auditors to assess how reliable information is and to seek more evidence about statements that may be incomplete or misleading. Weather records, insurance claims or count sheets would test the monsoon explanation. A signed statement is the runner-up, but it repeats the same person's words; evidence is more reliable when an independent source supplies it.

wrong_explanations.A: Writing an explanation down does not make it reliable. Skepticism means seeking evidence for what management says before relying on it.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it adds a document, but the source is unchanged. A statement signed by the manager does not corroborate the manager's own account.
wrong_explanations.D: A tripled write-off is an indicator, not proof. Saying the manager is concealing theft goes beyond what the evidence supports.

tips: Eliminate: A, because an unverified statement is not reliable evidence, and D, because one unexplained figure does not show that anyone stole.
Final two: B beats C because corroboration must come from a source other than the person explaining; a signature repeats the claim.
Exam cue: when a manager explains an oddity, the skeptical next step is independent evidence, neither trust nor accusation.

questions.subtopic: 1D3 Fraud risk management and red flags. A red flag management wants left out
questions.question: Internal auditor Sione finds falsified deposit slips at a Tongan credit union branch, and the branch manager, noting the money was repaid, asks that the matter go unreported. What is Sione's BEST course of action?

options.A: Leave the matter out now that the money is repaid
options.B: Keep it in the workpapers but out of the report
options.C: Report it through the route the organization's policies set
options.D: Notify the police directly that deposit records were falsified

questions.key_concept: A sign of fraud is reported through the channel that policy and law set; repayment or a manager's request does not change that.
questions.pre_read: Ask what repayment changes about the act itself, and who has the authority to decide what happens next.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.1 forbids internal auditors to conceal or omit findings, and Standards 1.2 and 1.3 require conduct that breaks ethical expectations or the law to be reported as policies and laws specify. Repayment does not undo the falsification. Keeping it in the workpapers is the runner-up, but a matter left out of communications is still kept from those who must act.

wrong_explanations.A: Repayment reduces the loss, not the act. Falsifying slips is deliberate deception, and Standard 1.1 forbids omitting it.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the facts are recorded, but workpapers reach nobody with authority to act. Leaving the matter out of communications is still omission.
wrong_explanations.D: Outside reporting follows what laws, regulations and policies specify. Going to the police alone skips the people the organization has authorized to act.

tips: Eliminate: A, because recovery of the money does not erase a deliberate falsification, and D, because outside reporting follows law and policy, not one auditor's choice.
Final two: C beats B because a finding kept in the workpapers but out of communications is still concealed from those with authority to act.
Exam cue: when someone asks an internal auditor to keep a red flag quiet, the answer is the set reporting channel.

questions.subtopic: 1D4 Controls that prevent and detect fraud. Telling a detective control from a preventive one
questions.question: Internal auditor Karim is classifying refund controls at an Egyptian electronics retailer in a risk and control matrix. Which control should Karim MOST appropriately record as detective?

options.A: A system limit that blocks refunds above a set amount
options.B: A rule that different staff enter and pay refunds
options.C: A supervisor's approval before each refund is paid out
options.D: A supervisor's weekly review of refunds already paid

questions.key_concept: Timing decides the type: a control that acts before the transaction completes prevents; one that looks afterward detects.
questions.pre_read: For each control, ask when it acts: before the refund is paid, or after.
questions.correct_explanation: A detective control finds a problem after it has happened. A weekly look at refunds already paid can reveal an improper refund only afterward; the CIA syllabus lists supervisory reviews among controls that detect fraud. The supervisor's approval before payment is the runner-up: the same person and a similar check, but it comes first, so it works as an authority level that prevents.

wrong_explanations.A: A system limit stops an oversized refund before it is paid. Stopping the event beforehand makes the control preventive.
wrong_explanations.B: Dividing entry and payment between different people removes the chance to act alone before any refund goes out, so it is preventive.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it involves a supervisor's check, but approval comes before payment. An authorization that can stop the transaction is preventive.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a blocking limit acts before the refund is paid, and B, because divided duties also work before the event.
Final two: D beats C because timing decides the type: approval before payment prevents, while review after payment detects.
Exam cue: ask when the control acts. Before the transaction completes it prevents; afterward it detects.

questions.subtopic: 1D4 Controls that prevent and detect fraud. Authority levels as prevention
questions.question: A monthly review at an Indonesian cement distributor found a buyer's orders far exceeded what the buyer was authorized to approve. Which control should internal auditor Putri recommend as BEST able to prevent a repeat?

options.A: A daily report of orders placed the previous day
options.B: System-enforced approval limits for each role
options.C: A hotline for staff to report purchasing concerns
options.D: A monthly reconciliation of orders to supplier invoices

questions.key_concept: Authority levels prevent fraud when they stop a transaction before it completes; reports, hotlines and reconciliations detect afterward.
questions.pre_read: The question says prevent. Ask which control acts before an order goes out.
questions.correct_explanation: A preventive control stops the transaction before it completes. When the system refuses an order above the user's limit, the oversized order is not placed; the CIA syllabus names authority levels as a way to prevent fraud. A daily report is the runner-up: it would catch the order sooner than the monthly review did, but after it was placed, so it still detects.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: faster than a monthly review, yet it still looks at orders already placed. Quicker detection is not prevention.
wrong_explanations.C: A hotline brings concerns to light after someone notices them. The syllabus lists whistleblower hotlines among controls that detect fraud.
wrong_explanations.D: A reconciliation compares records after the orders exist. It can reveal an oversized order but cannot stop one from being placed.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a hotline surfaces concerns after the act, and D, because a reconciliation compares records that already exist.
Final two: B beats A because an enforced limit blocks the order beforehand; a daily report shortens the time until it is found.
Exam cue: when the question says prevent, pick the control that acts before the transaction, usually an authorization or an enforced limit.

questions.subtopic: 1D4 Controls that prevent and detect fraud. Segregation of duties in a small team
questions.question: At a two-person field office of a Nepalese aid charity, one officer orders, receives and records fuel vouchers, and hiring is impossible. What should internal auditor Sunita recommend as the BEST response?

options.A: Management has the second officer review voucher records each week
options.B: Internal audit approves each voucher order until staffing levels improve
options.C: The officer certifies each month that no vouchers were misused
options.D: The charity relies on its yearly external audit to find misuse

questions.key_concept: Where duties cannot be separated, management adds an independent check; the internal auditor recommends it and does not operate it.
questions.pre_read: Ask who would be checking the officer's work under each option, and whether that person is independent and is management.
questions.correct_explanation: Controls are management's to design and run, and the IIA's position paper on fraud gives internal audit the role of assessing them. Where duties cannot be divided, a review by the second officer gives someone independent sight of the vouchers. Internal audit approving orders is the runner-up: it adds a second person, but it makes the auditor part of the process to be assessed later.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a second person does check each order, but approving transactions is a management responsibility. The auditor could not later assess that process objectively.
wrong_explanations.C: A person who could misuse vouchers cannot be the check on their own work. A control over one officer needs someone independent of that officer.
wrong_explanations.D: A yearly external audit is not a control over daily vouchers. It comes too late and is not designed to catch each misuse.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a check must be independent of the person checked, and D, because a yearly outside audit is not a control over daily transactions.
Final two: A beats B because management operates controls; an internal auditor who approves transactions takes on management's job and loses objectivity over it.
Exam cue: when duties cannot be separated, look for an independent review run by management, not by the internal auditor.

questions.subtopic: 1D4 Controls that prevent and detect fraud. Tone at the top and the likelihood of fraud
questions.question: Internal auditor Jurga finds that executives at a Lithuanian lender routinely waive approval limits for favored clients, although all staff signed the code of conduct. How should Jurga BEST reflect this when assessing engagement risks?

options.A: As proof that the executives are committing fraud
options.B: As a management prerogative outside the risk assessment
options.C: As a condition that raises the likelihood of fraud
options.D: As a risk the signed code of conduct already mitigates

questions.key_concept: Tone at the top is judged by what leaders do; leaders who set controls aside raise the likelihood of fraud.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the written rules say with what the leaders do, and ask which one staff will follow.
questions.correct_explanation: Tone at the top shows in what leaders do, and the CIA syllabus ties it to the likelihood of fraud. Executives who set controls aside signal that rules bend. Due professional care under Standard 4.2 includes weighing how probable fraud is, and this conduct makes it more probable. Relying on the signed code is the runner-up, but a code states intent; behavior at the top that contradicts it weakens the code.

wrong_explanations.A: Waiving limits is a warning sign, not proof. Concluding that fraud occurred needs evidence of intent and deception, established by an investigation.
wrong_explanations.B: Leaders can change limits through proper channels. Routinely setting them aside for favored clients is override, which belongs in the engagement risk assessment.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a signed code is a real control, but it shows intent. Leaders' conduct that contradicts it weakens the code for everyone.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a red flag is not proof of fraud, and B, because override by leaders is itself a risk to assess.
Final two: C beats D because tone is judged by leaders' actions; a signed code cannot offset executives who set controls aside.
Exam cue: when written ethics rules and leaders' behavior disagree, weigh the behavior; it raises the likelihood of fraud.

questions.subtopic: 1D5 Fraud investigation techniques and roles. What decides internal audit's investigation role
questions.question: After a hotline report alleges tuition fee theft at a Brazilian university, the board asks whether internal audit should investigate. Which consideration MOST determines the internal audit function's role?

options.A: Its independence from the managers of the university's fee office
options.B: Its mandate and its competencies for investigative work
options.C: The amount of money the report says was taken
options.D: The time left before the external audit begins

questions.key_concept: Whether internal audit investigates depends on its mandate and on having, or obtaining, the competencies; it is not automatic.
questions.pre_read: Ask two questions of each option: does it give authority to investigate, and does it give the skill?
questions.correct_explanation: Two things decide the role. The mandate must cover it: the considerations to Standard 6.1 give investigations as an example of a service a charter may name. And Standard 3.1 requires internal auditors to take on only services they have, or can obtain, the competencies for. Independence is the runner-up: it helps credibility, but it supplies neither authority nor investigative skill.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: independence matters for credibility, but it gives neither the authority nor the skill to investigate. Those come from the mandate and competencies.
wrong_explanations.C: The size of the loss affects urgency and resourcing, not whether investigating falls within internal audit's role.
wrong_explanations.D: The external audit's timetable is a scheduling matter. It does not show that internal audit is authorized or equipped to investigate.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the amount shapes urgency and not the role, and D, because another auditor's timetable gives internal audit no authority or skill.
Final two: B beats A because independence does not make an investigator; the mandate grants the role and competencies make it safe to perform.
Exam cue: asked whether internal audit investigates fraud, test two things: is it in the mandate, and are the competencies there?

questions.subtopic: 1D5 Fraud investigation techniques and roles. Competencies before investigative work
questions.question: A Philippine water utility's internal audit charter lists investigations, and internal auditor Luz, who has no investigative training, is assigned a suspected meter-reading fraud. What should Luz do FIRST?

options.A: Begin by interviewing the employees named in the allegation
options.B: Proceed on the authority the charter gives for investigations
options.C: Decline on the ground that investigating is outside internal audit
options.D: Ask the chief audit executive to obtain the needed competencies first

questions.key_concept: Authority in the charter is not enough: investigative work is taken on only with the competencies held or obtained.
questions.pre_read: The stem settles authority. Ask what is still missing before the work can start, and who can supply it.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 3.1 allows internal auditors to take on only services they have, or can obtain, the competencies for, and Standard 13.5 requires resource concerns to be discussed with the chief audit executive. The charter settles authority, not skill. Proceeding on the charter is the runner-up, but the IIA's position paper on fraud warns that an unskilled investigation can spoil evidence or accuse the wrong person.

wrong_explanations.A: Interviewing people named in an allegation is investigative work. Without training it risks a wrongful accusation and damaged evidence, the dangers the position paper names.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the mandate is one of two tests. The charter authorizes the service, but the competencies must also be held or obtained.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal audit may investigate when its mandate covers it and the skills are there or can be obtained. The gap calls for resourcing, not refusal.

tips: Eliminate: A, because interviewing is itself investigative work needing skill, and C, because investigating is allowed where mandate and competencies exist.
Final two: D beats B because authority in the charter does not supply competence; skills must be held or obtained before the work starts.
Exam cue: mandate answers 'may we?', competency answers 'can we?'. When skills are missing, the gap goes to the chief audit executive.

questions.subtopic: 1D5 Fraud investigation techniques and roles. Using investigators' information in planning
questions.question: Planning an engagement on passenger refunds at a Portuguese airline, internal auditor Tiago learns that the investigations unit closed six refund cases last year. What is the BEST use of that information?

options.A: Treat refunds as already covered and remove them from the engagement scope
options.B: Set the closed cases aside as matters already resolved
options.C: Feed the case patterns into the engagement risk assessment
options.D: Share the case details with the refunds manager before fieldwork

questions.key_concept: Investigators' past cases, trends and complaints are planning input: they show where a process has been exposed to fraud.
questions.pre_read: Ask what six closed cases say about the process, and what the investigators did and did not examine.
questions.correct_explanation: Past cases show which schemes were tried and which controls failed, so they point to exposure in the refund process. The considerations to Standard 13.2 list reviewing risk assessments made by others and meeting other providers as ways to gather planning information, and the CIA syllabus names prior investigations and trends. Dropping refunds from scope is the runner-up, but six cases argue for more attention, not less.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the unit's work is relevant, but it examined specific cases. It gave no assurance that refund controls now work, and six cases signal exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: Closed cases still show how fraud was committed and which controls failed. That is direct planning input on where the process is exposed.
wrong_explanations.D: Investigation details are confidential and are shared as policy and law allow. Planning needs the patterns; the manager has no need for the files.

tips: Eliminate: B, because closed cases still reveal schemes and failed controls, and D, because investigation details are protected information, shared as policy and law allow.
Final two: C beats A because investigators examined individual cases; their findings inform the risk assessment and do not replace assurance over the process.
Exam cue: investigators' risk assessments, past cases, trends and complaints are planning input for the internal auditor.

questions.subtopic: 1D5 Fraud investigation techniques and roles. Internal audit's part after a fraud
questions.question: An outside forensic firm has finished investigating a payroll fraud at a Jamaican hotel group and reported to the board. What is the internal audit function's MOST appropriate contribution now?

options.A: Assess how the payroll controls failed and recommend improvements
options.B: Put stronger payroll controls in place before the next pay run
options.C: Decide the disciplinary action for the employees involved
options.D: Repeat the whole investigation to confirm the forensic firm's findings

questions.key_concept: After a fraud, internal audit works out how the controls failed and recommends improvements; management implements them.
questions.pre_read: Sort the options by who should act: management, the investigators or the internal audit function.
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's position paper on fraud gives internal audit a part once a fraud has happened: it should work out how the controls failed, point to improvements, and consider whether similar problems are likely elsewhere. Acting on the recommendations is management's work. Putting new controls in place is the runner-up: the right goal, but done by the wrong party, and it would leave internal audit assessing its own work.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: stronger controls are needed, but management designs and operates them. An internal auditor who installs controls cannot later assess them objectively.
wrong_explanations.C: Discipline is a decision for management, advised by human resources and legal counsel. Internal audit reports facts and does not sanction staff.
wrong_explanations.D: Qualified specialists have investigated and reported. Redoing their work adds cost without a reason to doubt it, and it is not internal audit's part.

tips: Eliminate: C, because sanctions are management's decision, and D, because a completed specialist investigation is not redone without cause.
Final two: A beats B because internal audit assesses and recommends, while management implements; the auditor who builds a control cannot assess it later.
Exam cue: after a fraud, internal audit asks how the controls failed and what should improve; management fixes and disciplines.
